sources.news_title: Georgia man fakes medical emergency to avoid paying Red Lobster bill, police allege
Georgia man calls 911 from a Red Lobster, says he has a medical emergency. Then the police takes him into custody for 'unlawful conduct'
sources.text:
What was meant to be a routine seafood dinner turned into a bizarre criminal case in Douglas County, Georgia. Abdul Hakeem Rasheed, a 26-year-old resident, was arrested after police say he faked a medical crisis and personally called emergency services in what investigators believe was an attempt to avoid paying his restaurant tab.
The incident, which took place at a local Red Lobster, has drawn attention because of the extreme lengths the diner allegedly went to over a bill totaling less than $64.
The bizarre chain of events unfolded on the evening of Sept. 24. According to People, an arrest affidavit obtained from the Douglas Police Department states that Rasheed was dining at the Red Lobster restaurant when it was time to settle his bill.
The fraudulent scheme can carry serious consequences
Rather than providing a standard method of payment, investigators allege that Rasheed came up with an exit strategy based on deception.
According to local authorities, Rasheed began showing signs of physical distress inside the restaurant, apparently to make it look like he was experiencing a sudden and serious medical episode. To further support the ruse, Rasheed personally placed an emergency call, telling dispatchers that he was in immediate need of medical attention.
However, arriving emergency responders and law enforcement officers quickly became suspicious of the situation. A deeper investigation by responding officers allegedly revealed that the reason for the emergency call was not a medical problem, but the unpaid bill sitting at Rasheed’s table. The total cost of the meal was exactly $63.77.
The following day, Friday, Sept. 25, Rasheed was taken into custody by the Douglas Police Department and booked into the local detention facility. Court records show that he is facing two misdemeanor charges related to the incident: theft of services and unlawful conduct during an emergency call.
The affidavit filed by investigators says Rasheed engaged in “unlawful conduct” during the emergency call “by deception and with intent to avoid payment.”
In Georgia, using the emergency response system for a non-emergency situation or as part of a fraudulent scheme can carry serious consequences. The law reflects concerns about emergency resources being diverted from people facing actual life-threatening situations.
His bond was set at $3,000
Following his booking, a judge set Rasheed’s bond at $3,000. Online jail records show that he has been unable to post the required amount and remains in custody at the Douglas County Jail.
While dine-and-dash incidents are a common headache for restaurant managers, allegedly fabricating a medical emergency takes the situation into a different territory because of the emergency response involved. Every ambulance or police cruiser sent to a false emergency is potentially unavailable for a genuine stroke, car accident, violent crime or another situation where someone actually needs help.
Representatives for Red Lobster and the Douglas Police Department have not yet released formal statements regarding the arrest. Rasheed’s initial court dates are expected to be scheduled in the coming weeks, where he will face the legal consequences of an alleged exit strategy that resulted in a $3,000 bond over a $63.77 dinner bill.

sources.news_title: Cheddar Bay Flunk-Out: Georgia Diner Dials 911 On Fake Medical Emergency To Dodge $64 Red Lobster Tab
Nigerian arrested for calling 911 to dodge meal bill
sources.text:
A Nigerian man, Abdul Rasheed, has been arrested after calling 911 and faking illness to avoid paying a bill of $63 Lobster meal in a restaurant in the United States.
Rasheed confessed that he attempted to escape paying the bill of the meal he ate as a customer at a Red Lobster restaurant in Douglas County, Georgia.
According to a report by New York Post on Friday, the Nigerian was apprehended last Thursday.
Consequently, he was booked into the Douglas County Jail on allegations of theft of services and unlawful conduct during a 911 call.
He was being held on a $3,000 bond.
“Law enforcement sources said Rasheed had finished a $63 meal at the restaurant before allegedly deciding that he would rather not settle the bill,” the report stated.
Authorities said he then called 911 and claimed he was sick while requesting medical assistance to make him dodge the payment for the bill.
He was found completely well when emergency responders arrived in his home, but unwilling to pay for his meal.
“Instead of an ambulance trip to the hospital, he got a Very Important Person ride in the back of a police car to Douglas County Jail,” it added.

BS BULLETIN:
- Police say a Georgia diner faked a medical emergency after getting a roughly $63 bill at Red Lobster.
- The 26-year-old allegedly called 911 hoping to avoid paying.
- Emergency responders found him medically fine — and police took him to jail instead.
A Georgia man apparently decided there was only one way out of a $63 Red Lobster bill.
Call 911.
Police say 26-year-old Abdul Rasheed was dining at a Red Lobster on Highway 5 in Douglasville on Sept. 24 when he allegedly tried to fake a medical emergency rather than pay his tab.
Rasheed himself called 911, according to Douglasville police. That brought emergency responders to the restaurant. There was just one problem.
Police say Rasheed was fine.
What officers did find, according to authorities, was a diner who apparently hoped the supposed emergency would get him out of paying for his meal. It did not.
Rasheed was arrested and booked into the Douglas County Jail.
WSB-TV, citing Douglasville police, reported that he was charged with theft of services, unlawful conduct during a 911 call and making a false report.
Other reporting based on jail records lists the tab at $63.77 and shows bonds totaling $4,500.

sources.news_title: A Georgia man called 911 claiming a medical emergency, then police say it was all to avoid paying for dinner
sources.text:
Police in Georgia say a man pretended to need emergency medical care and dialed 911 so he could leave a Red Lobster without settling a $63.77 dinner tab, according to People. The man, 26, named in the affidavit as Abdul Hakeem Rasheed, is accused of reporting a false medical emergency during a meal at the restaurant on Sept. 24. The outlet obtained the document.
The affidavit alleges that Rasheed displayed “unlawful conduct” during the call “by deception and with intent to avoid payment.” Jail records the outlet reviewed show he was booked on Sept. 25, facing a theft-of-services count and an unlawful-conduct count tied to the 911 call. The outlet said it had sought responses from the police department and the restaurant chain.
The restaurant is on Georgia Highway 5 in Douglasville, in Douglas County, according to the Douglas County Sentinel, which cited documents from the Douglasville Police Department. That report said police determined the call was false and meant to help him leave without paying.
Bond status and Georgia law
Accounts of his custody status differ. People cited a $3,000 bond and said he remained in jail, while the local paper reported a $4,500 bond and said he had been released. Georgia’s theft-of-services law, Georgia Code § 16-8-5, reads: “A person commits the offense of theft of services when by deception and with the intent to avoid payment he knowingly obtains services, accommodations, entertainment, or the use of personal property which is available only for compensation.” The wording in the affidavit closely mirrors that statute.
The state’s penalty section, Georgia Code § 16-8-12, says a person convicted under the theft-of-services section “shall be punished as for a misdemeanor” with listed exceptions. The exceptions that carry prison terms apply to property worth $1,500.01 or more and to certain repeat theft convictions. The bill here was far below that figure.
A separate law, Georgia Code § 16-11-39.2, addresses misuse of 911 calls. One listed act reads: “Calls or otherwise contacts 911 and makes a false report.” Another is contacting 911 “for the purpose of interfering with or disrupting emergency telephone service.” The section also lists using “obscene, vulgar, or profane language” to intimidate or harass a 911 communications officer.
Those provisions are separate from the false-report paragraph. A violation of the section is a misdemeanor, punishable by “a fine of not more than $500.00 or 12 months in jail, or both.” The reports reviewed do not say which provision of that law Rasheed is accused of violating. An arrest and an affidavit are allegations, and he is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.
Published: Oct 3, 2026 07:30 am

sources.news_title: Man Allegedly Fakes Medical Emergency to Skip $63 Red Lobster Tab, Gets Arrested Instead
sources.text:
Somebody out here really looked at a $63 Red Lobster check and decided the best move was to dial 911. Over some shrimp!
Abdul Rasheed, a 26-year-old from Douglasville, Georgia, is now facing a pile of criminal charges after cops say he called 911 on Sept. 24 from the Red Lobster on Highway 5 in hopes of dodging the bill. Officers rolled up expecting a real emergency and, according to police, found Rasheed was OK, but he was hoping to avoid his $63 bill…
RELATED: Man Arrested for Stalking and Producing Fake Marriage License with Victim’s Name
Law enforcement sources say the man had already put away a full meal before the check hit the table. When the bill came, it left a bad taste in his mouth, and he cooked up a scheme to get a free meal. The plan, allegedly, was to call 911 and pretend he was sick while requesting medical attention.
The idea seems to have been that an ambulance run would pull him out the door before the server could say “will that be cash or card?” Instead, the folks who showed up weren’t buying it. Instead of an ambulance trip, Rasheed got an exclusive ride in the back of a cop car.
The plot twist is that the check he was running from may be the cheapest part of this whole situation. Police arrested Rasheed and charged him with theft of services, unlawful conduct during a 911 call and making a false report. He was booked into the Douglas County Jail.
According to Globe, a judge set Rasheed’s bond at $1,500 for the theft of service charge and $3,000 for the unlawful conduct during a 9-1-1 call charge, so he’s looking at $4,500 to avoid paying a $63 bill at Red Lobster. That’s about 71 times the price of the meal. Records show he is still being held in custody at the Douglas County Jail.

According to authorities, Rasheed had finished his meal at the restaurant on Bill Arp Road when the bill came due. He allegedly called 911 and requested medical assistance, prompting a response from law enforcement.

Responding officers determined Rasheed was not experiencing a medical emergency, according to authorities, and the incident instead resulted in criminal charges.

The Red Lobster is located at 3100 Bill Arp Road near Highway 5 and Interstate 20, about 20 miles west of downtown Atlanta. Douglasville, the county seat of Douglas County, is part of the Atlanta metropolitan area.

sources.text:
In a bizarre incident that highlights the lengths some individuals will go to avoid payment, a man named Abdul Rasheed was arrested after he called 911 from a Red Lobster in Douglasville, Georgia, claiming a medical emergency. According to the Douglasville police, Rasheed’s actions were a ploy to evade a $63 bill for his meal. When officers arrived at the scene, they found that Rasheed was in good health, contradicting his emergency claim.
This unusual event underscores not only the misuse of emergency services but also the consequences of attempting to defraud a business. Rasheed was subsequently charged with making a false report, a serious offense that can divert police resources from genuine emergencies. The incident serves as a cautionary tale about the legal repercussions of attempting to dodge financial responsibilities through deceitful means.
The broader implications of this case reflect ongoing discussions about the integrity of emergency services and the importance of reserving such resources for actual emergencies. In a time when first responders are stretched thin, incidents like this can undermine public trust and safety. This situation also raises awareness among restaurant owners and patrons alike about the potential for similar fraudulent behavior, prompting them to remain vigilant in ensuring that all patrons honor their bills.
